message.content:
Using local_dev flag on a none cli repo would allow entire to setup git hooks that then could execute what ever is in the bash script in that repo. This is an issue for anyone installing a random repo and potentially entire enabling the git hooks. In theor localdev should only be for the cli repo but it also has it risk there since checking out a branch might also just execute what ever script is in there.

So I think local_dev needs to go away. But before we do that can we brain storm if there is a safe way to dogfood the cli code when using an agent in the cli repo?

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

#!/bin/sh
# Entire CLI local-development hook launcher.
#
# In local-dev mode, Entire hooks invoke the CLI straight from source via
# "go run", which recompiles on demand. When the tree does not compile (for
# example while an agent is resolving a merge conflict) "go run" fails and the
# hook would silently do nothing. This launcher first checks that the tree
# builds; if it does it runs the freshly compiled CLI, otherwise it falls back
# to an "entire" binary on PATH. If neither is available it exits 0 so it never
# blocks the surrounding git or agent operation.
#
# Usage: scripts/entire-dev <entire args...>
#
# All local-dev hooks delegate here so the build-probe-and-fallback logic lives
# in one place rather than being duplicated across generated hook commands.

set -eu

# Informational messages go to stderr so they never pollute hook stdout (some
# hooks emit JSON there).
log() {
	printf '[entire-dev] %s\n' "$1" >&2
}

# Resolve the repository root from this script's own location so it works
# regardless of the caller's working directory. Parameter expansion avoids
# depending on external tools like dirname, which may not be on PATH when this
# runs from a minimal hook environment.
case "$0" in
	*/*) script_dir=${0%/*} ;;
	*) script_dir=. ;;
esac
root=$(CDPATH= cd -- "$script_dir/.." && pwd)
# Build/run the whole cmd/entire package, not just main.go: package main is
# split across multiple files (e.g. the git-remote-entire dispatch in
# remotehelper.go), and naming a single file would leave the others out and
# fail to compile.
pkg="$root/cmd/entire"

# Run freshly compiled code when the tree builds. The build probe populates the
# build cache, so the subsequent "go run" does not recompile from scratch.
if command -v go >/dev/null 2>&1 && go build -o /dev/null "$pkg" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	exec go run "$pkg" "$@"
fi

# The tree does not build (or Go is unavailable): fall back to the installed
# binary so hooks keep working while the source is broken.
if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	log "project isn't compiling; falling back to the entire binary on PATH"
	exec entire "$@"
fi

# Nothing to run: do not block the surrounding operation.
log "project isn't compiling and no entire binary on PATH; skipping hook"
exit 0

docs/architecture/external-commands.md:154:Resolution is **install-time only** — dispatch stays zero-cost. The outcome is verified, not just the attempt: an install that lands below the requirement's `min_version` fails with both versions named, because the install takes the newest published tag and that tag may still be too old. Reporting success there would defeat the guarantee the plan was built on. After installing the main plugin, missing dependencies are resolved transitively (metadata-only, nothing downloaded during planning; a per-name record of the strictest `min_version` seen, plus a depth bound, make metadata cycles an error rather than a hang), listed apt-style, and installed after one confirmation (`--yes` skips, `--no-deps` opts out). The listing carries no per-entry trust annotation, because there is no longer a path by which an author-chosen URL can appear in it: a missing dependency comes from the index, and an upgrade reinstalls from the source that plugin's own install already accepted. A declined plan is a warning, not a failure. Dependencies already satisfied from raw `$PATH` or a local-dev install count as satisfied, with a warning when `min_version` can't be verified.
docs/architecture/external-commands.md:159:- `entire plugin doctor` reports missing/outdated dependencies, manifest/bin-dir drift, binaries that no longer match the `binary_sha256` recorded at install, installs that were never checksum-verified, dangling local-dev symlinks, and (macOS) a `com.apple.quarantine` attribute that would block execution. Exit code 1 when issues are found. The integrity check covers the `pkg/` binary the manifest describes; where `bin/` holds a copy rather than a link (Windows without Developer Mode), the dangling/non-executable link check is what guards that surface.

content.text:
Confirmed the mechanism. Before the options, three findings that sharpen the framing:

**1. The exposure is live in this repo, and needs no victim flag.** `.entire/settings.json` is a tracked file and it commits `local_dev: true` (line 3). `local_dev` is merged from the *project* scope — `mergeScalarFields` reads it from whichever file it appears in (`settings/settings.go:959`), and `Load` layers project → clone-prefs → local (`settings.go:449`). So any repo can commit `local_dev: true`; a victim who clones it and runs `entire enable` gets git hooks and agent hooks that execute `./scripts/entire-dev` from that repo. Worse, `strategy/common.go:111` re-installs the git hook from merged settings on its own, so the committed value keeps regenerating the dev hook without anyone passing a flag.

**2. Two exposures are tangled here, and only one is a bug.**
- *Repo-controlled activation* — a tracked file decides that hooks execute repo content. That's the security bug, and it has nothing to do with dogfooding.
- *Working-tree execution* — even correctly activated, hooks `go run ./cmd/entire` from the tree, so `git checkout <pr-branch>` + any commit runs that branch's code. That's inherent to "run from source." It's a trust decision, not a bug — but it should be explicit and per-machine.

**3. `local_dev` is bad dogfooding anyway.** Production hook commands are wrapped (`sh -c 'if ! command -v entire …; then exit 0; fi; exec …'`, `agent/hook_command.go:93`); local-dev commands are not wrapped at all (`claudecode/hooks.go:161-186`). Local-dev also gets a bespoke 60s SessionEnd timeout production never has (`claudecode/hooks.go:71`). So the divergence sits exactly in the fragile part — PATH probing, wrapper quoting, hook timeouts. Every hour spent in local-dev mode is an hour *not* testing the hook shape users actually get. Removing it improves fidelity.

## Options

**A. PATH shadowing via a built binary — my recommendation.** `mise run dev:publish` already exists and installs `entire` + `git-remote-entire` into `~/go/bin`. Production hooks say plain `entire`, resolved through PATH. So a dev build on PATH means: hook scripts byte-identical to what ships, running your code. Warm build is 1.3s, so a rebuild-per-change is real but small. Trust boundary is "what's on my PATH" — already the developer's own domain, unreachable by repo content or branch checkout.

*Gap to close:* knowing whether the binary on PATH matches your tree. Stamp dev builds with short SHA + dirty marker and surface it in `entire status`/`version`; optionally a `mise run dev:watch` (fswatch/entr around `dev:publish`) to make the rebuild invisible. Note the scope change: this shadows `entire` for *every* repo on your machine, not just this one — which is arguably the point (broader dogfooding), but the staleness signal becomes important.

**B. Pinned runner worktree — best answer to the branch-checkout problem, if you want source-freshness.** Hooks point at an absolute path into a separate worktree you update deliberately. Checking out a PR branch in your working worktree can't change what the hooks execute. Cost: an extra worktree, and it dogfoods *main* rather than your in-progress change. That split is defensible — dogfood main continuously to catch regressions early, and test in-progress changes through the existing `test-repo` skill / e2e harness, which already spawn the real binary with isolated config and are more representative than this repo (which is atypical: odd checkpoint remote, `local_dev`, etc.).

**C. If you want to keep a source-run dev mode at all**, the minimum safe shape is three changes: activation moves somewhere version control cannot reach — `~/.config/entire/` (there's already `userdirs.Config()` as the single resolver) or clone preferences in the git common dir (already a settings layer, untracked by definition) — and it should be an **allowlist of absolute repo paths**, so only repos you named get it; the launcher moves out of the repo (a repo-relative launcher path is the sharpest edge); and `local_dev` in a tracked project file must be *rejected with a warning*, not merely ignored, or the existing committed one and every other repo's stay live.

I'd take A, with B if the auto-freshness turns out to matter more than expected. A is the only one that also *improves* what you're testing.

## For the removal PR — things that don't close on their own

- **Deleting the field doesn't disarm existing machines.** Hooks already installed still contain `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/scripts/entire-dev`. `entireHookPrefixes` does recognize the local-dev prefixes for removal/upgrade (`claudecode/hooks.go:74-80`), so make sure a plain `entire enable` rewrites stale local-dev hooks rather than only `--force` doing it. Same for the git hook (`localDevHookCmdPrefix = "./scripts/entire-dev"`, `strategy/hooks.go:30`).
- **Delete `scripts/entire-dev`** with it. Leaving the script leaves the payload.
- **Drop `local_dev` from this repo's `.entire/settings.json`** — one line, removes the live exposure immediately, independent of the larger removal.
- **`entire agent add --local-dev` is not hidden** (`agent_group.go:124`), unlike the hidden flags in `setup.go:788,957`. And `install-hooks [--local-dev]` is part of the documented external-agent protocol (`docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md:213`), so removal is a third-party contract change and needs a deprecation story rather than a straight delete.
- ~274 references across the tree, heavily in `setup_test.go`, where `local_dev` is the stand-in for "local-only field that must not leak into project scope." Those tests are testing scope isolation, not local-dev — they'll need a different local-only field (`log_level` or `absolute_git_hook_path`) rather than deletion, or you lose that coverage.

Want me to write this up as a plan, or start with the one-line removal of `local_dev` from this repo's settings to close the live exposure first?

content.text:
Your instinct is right to probe it, and the answer is that **B shouldn't point hooks at the worktree at all** — the immutability comes from copying the binary out, not from a clever pointer. A pinned runner worktree is a *build source*, not a runtime target: build from it → install to a stable location outside every repo → hooks reference that the ordinary way. A branch checkout in your dev worktree changes nothing because the bytes were already copied. That means B needs zero new hook plumbing, and it composes with A rather than competing with it.

That reframe matters because a pointer *can't* be made tamper-proof here. The two hook surfaces have opposite integrity properties:

| surface | file | tracked? | branch checkout can swap it? |
|---|---|---|---|
| git hooks | `.git/hooks/*` (`GetHooksDir`) | no — inside `.git/` | **no** |
| agent hooks | `.claude/settings.json` (`claudecode/hooks.go:103`) | **yes, in this repo** | **yes** |

- **Git hooks are already in the safe place** and already have the strongest available form: `--absolute-git-hook-path` inlines a shell-quoted absolute path at install time (`hooks.go:468-490`) with *no runtime config lookup* — the script literally contains `/Users/soph/…/entire hooks …`. Nothing in the repo can redirect it.
- **Agent hooks are unfixable from entire's side.** Entire writes them into a tracked file, so the hook command string *is* version-controlled content — a checkout rewrites it regardless of what you put there. And there's no absolute-path mode for agent hooks at all: `AbsoluteGitHookPath`/`os.Executable` appear nowhere under `cmd/entire/cli/agent/`. Whether to trust project-settings hooks is Claude Code's decision, not entire's.

So the only thing entire actually controls for agent hooks is *what the command string names* — and naming a stable binary outside the repo (plain `entire` on PATH) beats naming repo content (`${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/scripts/entire-dev}`). That's the entire win, and it needs no pointer.

**Concretely, B:**
1. Pinned runner worktree (`~/.entire-runner`) on main or a known-good tag, updated deliberately (`git -C ~/.entire-runner pull`).
2. A `dev:publish` variant that builds *from* the runner worktree into `~/go/bin`.
3. Agent hooks stay plain `entire` → PATH → runner build. Byte-identical to production, so you keep the wrapper-fidelity win. Git hooks likewise, or `--absolute-git-hook-path` if you want PATH-independence for GUI git clients.

The deliberate trade-off: you dogfood the runner's *commit*, not your uncommitted edits — which is why it pairs with the test-repo/e2e path for in-progress work.

**One lever worth closing while you're in here:** `absolute_git_hook_path` is read from merged settings including the tracked project file (`hookSettingsFromConfig` → `settings.Load`), and `common.go:110-113` silently re-installs git hooks from it whenever the hook is missing. Far more benign than `local_dev` — the inlined path is `os.Executable()`, an entire binary the user already ran, not repo content — but it's the same shape. Worth adopting as a rule: **no tracked setting may influence hook command generation.** Both fields become local/clone-scope only, rejected with a warning in project scope.

And the honest limit: none of this defends against code already running as you in the repo — an agent, a malicious `//go:generate`, or a test can rewrite `.git/hooks/*` or `~/go/bin/entire` directly. No pointer design fixes that, so don't buy complexity for it. The achievable bar is exactly **(a) no tracked file activates anything, (b) an ordinary branch checkout swaps no executed code**. A and B both clear it; `local_dev` fails both.

Want me to draft the removal plan with that rule as the invariant, or prototype the runner-worktree mise task first?

name: Nightly Release

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # 06:00 UTC daily
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: nightly-release-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  create-nightly-tag:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Generate token
        id: app-token
        uses: actions/create-github-app-token@bcd2ba49218906704ab6c1aa796996da409d3eb1 # v3.2.0
        with:
          app-id: ${{ secrets.HOMEBREW_TAP_APP_ID }}
          private-key: ${{ secrets.HOMEBREW_TAP_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          owner: ${{ github.repository_owner }}
          repositories: cli

      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          token: ${{ steps.app-token.outputs.token }}

      - name: Create nightly tag
        run: |
          TAG=$(scripts/create-nightly-tag.sh) && EXIT_CODE=0 || EXIT_CODE=$?
          if [ "$EXIT_CODE" -eq 2 ]; then
            echo "Skipping — no new nightly needed."
            exit 0
          elif [ "$EXIT_CODE" -ne 0 ] || [ -z "$TAG" ]; then
            echo "::error::Failed to generate nightly tag"
            exit 1
          fi
          git tag "$TAG"
          git push origin "$TAG"

=== create-nightly-tag.sh ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Calculate the next nightly release tag based on the latest stable tag and HEAD.
# Outputs the tag name to stdout, or exits 0 silently if a nightly already exists for HEAD.
#
# Tag format: v<major>.<minor>.<patch+1>-nightly.<YYYYMMDDhhmm>.<short-commit>
# Usage: scripts/create-nightly-tag.sh

SHORT_COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

# Skip if a nightly tag already exists for this commit
if git tag -l "v*-nightly.*.${SHORT_COMMIT}" | grep -q .; then
  echo "Nightly tag already exists for commit ${SHORT_COMMIT}, skipping." >&2
  exit 2
fi

# Find the latest stable version tag (exclude prereleases)
LATEST_STABLE=$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 --match 'v[0-9]*' --exclude '*-*' 2>/dev/null)
if [ -z "$LATEST_STABLE" ]; then
  echo "::error::No stable version tag found" >&2
  exit 1
fi

# Bump patch version: v0.5.4 → v0.5.5
MAJOR=$(echo "$LATEST_STABLE" | sed 's/^v//' | cut -d. -f1)
MINOR=$(echo "$LATEST_STABLE" | sed 's/^v//' | cut -d. -f2)
PATCH=$(echo "$LATEST_STABLE" | sed 's/^v//' | cut -d. -f3)
NEXT_PATCH=$((PATCH + 1))
NIGHTLY_VERSION="v${MAJOR}.${MINOR}.${NEXT_PATCH}"

DATE=$(TZ=UTC0 date +%Y%m%d%H%M)
TAG="${NIGHTLY_VERSION}-nightly.${DATE}.${SHORT_COMMIT}"

# Skip if this exact tag already exists
if git rev-parse "${TAG}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "Tag ${TAG} already exists, skipping." >&2
  exit 2
fi

echo "${TAG}"

content.text:
Confirmed all three mise features exist in 2026.8.5. And the headline: **you don't need to build this — the pipeline already does it, on a cron instead of on merge.**

Three pieces already fit together:

- `scripts/install.sh --channel nightly` already installs the latest nightly (`install.sh:115-124`, `195-207`).
- `create-nightly-tag.sh` is **already commit-idempotent** — it exits 2 if a nightly tag exists for HEAD (`create-nightly-tag.sh:13-17`). So running it per-push is safe: main hasn't moved → no tag, no release.
- `release.yml` fires on `push: tags: v*` → goreleaser builds and publishes. And nightly tags are prereleases, so `experimental.Visible` stays `"true"` — dogfooding sees the experimental surface, exactly as CLAUDE.md describes.

So "build on every main update" is a trigger change to `nightly.yml`, not new machinery.

**But trigger on green CI, not raw push.** `push: branches: [main]` fires in parallel with `ci.yml`, so you'd publish dev builds of untested commits — bad for something people install. Use the CI run's completion instead:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["CI"]
    types: [completed]
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"   # keep as a safety net
  workflow_dispatch:
```
…with a `if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'` guard on the job. Also worth a look: the existing `concurrency: cancel-in-progress: true` on group `nightly-release-${{ github.ref }}` means rapid merges cancel each other. Tag creation is fast and idempotent so the risk is low, but `cancel-in-progress: false` is the safer default here.

**This also retires the runner worktree — and is strictly safer than it.** A local runner still runs `go build` over code you fetched; CI moves that compile off your laptop into a sandbox. You also gain fidelity: you're testing goreleaser's actual binary, the real install path, and the real version stamping, none of which a bare `go build` exercises. Same argument that killed `local_dev`, applied one level up.

**Where mise fits — a small, appropriate role:**

```toml
[tasks."dev:sync"]
description = "Install the latest nightly (dogfood main)"
run = "scripts/install.sh --channel nightly"

[hooks]
enter = "mise run dev:sync"   # ⚠ throttle — see below
```

`sources`/`outputs` give you make-like staleness so the task no-ops when nothing changed. Two cautions: `install.sh` hits the GitHub API **unauthenticated** (60 req/hr), so an unconditional `enter` hook will rate-limit you — gate it on a timestamp file for once-per-hour. And `mise watch` is the wrong tool here: it watches local files, but the event you care about is "origin/main moved," which no local watcher can see.

**Honest caveats:**
- **Latency** — merge → CI green → tag → goreleaser → publish is probably 10–20 min. Good for catching regressions in main; useless for iterating on your own in-progress change, which stays on the test-repo/e2e path.
- **Release volume** — one prerelease per merge. At 20 merges/day that's 20 GitHub releases; you'll want a pruning policy, and note `get_latest_nightly_version` does `grep nightly | head -n 1` over the releases list.
- This composes with the earlier decision cleanly: hooks say plain `entire`, PATH resolves to the installed nightly. No pointer, no worktree, nothing in the repo influencing what runs.

So the full picture is now: **remove `local_dev`, hooks stay on the production `entire`/PATH shape, and dogfooding main becomes a CI trigger flip plus a one-task `dev:sync`.** Want me to write that up as the removal plan, or start with the `nightly.yml` trigger change since it's independent and low-risk?

import pathlib, re
p = pathlib.Path("cmd/entire/cli/agent/codex/hooks_test.go")
s = p.read_text()
m = re.search(r'func TestInstallHooks_LocalDev\(t \*testing\.T\) \{.*?\n\}\n', s, re.S)
new = '''func TestInstallHooks_ReplacesLegacyLocalDevHook(t *testing.T) {
	tempDir := setupTestEnv(t)
	ctx := context.Background()
	ag := &CodexAgent{}

	_, err := ag.InstallHooks(ctx, false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	// Rewrite the installed command into the shape local-dev mode used to write:
	// a script inside the working tree. Editing the raw file keeps this
	// independent of the config struct layout. hooks.json stores commands as
	// JSON strings, so the quotes in the legacy command arrive escaped.
	hooksPath := filepath.Join(tempDir, ".codex", HooksFileName)
	prod := agent.WrapProductionSilentHookCommandForOS("entire hooks codex stop", agent.UseWindowsProductionHooks(ctx))
	legacy := agent.LegacyLocalDevHookScript + " hooks codex stop"
	raw, err := os.ReadFile(hooksPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	encode := func(s string) string {
		b, err := json.Marshal(s)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		return string(b[1 : len(b)-1]) // strip the surrounding quotes
	}
	seeded := strings.Replace(string(raw), encode(prod), encode(legacy), 1)
	require.NotEqual(t, string(raw), seeded, "could not find the installed stop command to seed the legacy hook")
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(hooksPath, []byte(seeded), 0o600))

	// A plain install (no --force) must replace the legacy hook rather than add
	// the binary hook alongside it: two hooks would both fire, and the
	// repo-relative one would keep running whatever the branch contains.
	_, err = ag.InstallHooks(ctx, false)
	require.NoError(t, err)

	after, err := os.ReadFile(hooksPath)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NotContains(t, string(after), "scripts/entire-dev", "legacy local-dev hook survived a non-force install")
	require.Equal(t, 1, strings.Count(string(after), encode(prod)), "current hook must appear exactly once")
}
'''
s = s[:m.start()] + new + s[m.end():]
p.write_text(s)
print("ok")

content.subject: Remove localDev from strategy git-hook generation

content.subject: Change Agent.InstallHooks signature across all agents
content.description: InstallHooks(ctx, localDev, force) -> InstallHooks(ctx, force) in agent.Agent interface and all 8 agent impls plus external/capabilities. Remove localDev branches; keep legacy prefix detection.

content.subject: Keep legacy local-dev prefix detection for hook rewrite
content.description: Retain the local-dev/go-run hook command prefixes in each agent's entireHookPrefixes (as legacy detection constants) so already-installed local-dev hooks are recognized and rewritten rather than left armed on developer machines.

content.subject: Remove --local-dev flags and EnableOptions.LocalDev
content.description: Remove flagLocalDev const, hidden flags in setup.go, visible flag on `entire agent add`, EnableOptions.LocalDev field, and stop passing --local-dev to external agents.

content.subject: Update docs and run fmt/lint/test:ci

content.subject: Fix migration gap: strip stale Entire hooks without --force
content.description: cursor, factoryaidroid, claudecode, copilotcli only call removeEntireHooks when force=true, so a plain `entire enable` adds the production hook while leaving a legacy local-dev hook in place — both fire, and the repo-relative launcher keeps executing. Make removal of stale (non-current) Entire hooks unconditional, matching codex's syncHookCommand. Must stay idempotent (count 0 when already current) and never touch foreign hooks.

docs/architecture/external-commands.md:154:Resolution is **install-time only** — dispatch stays zero-cost. The outcome is verified, not just the attempt: an install that lands below the requirement's `min_version` fails with both versions named, because the install takes the newest published tag and that tag may still be too old. Reporting success there would defeat the guarantee the plan was built on. After installing the main plugin, missing dependencies are resolved transitively (metadata-only, nothing downloaded during planning; a per-name record of the strictest `min_version` seen, plus a depth bound, make metadata cycles an error rather than a hang), listed apt-style, and installed after one confirmation (`--yes` skips, `--no-deps` opts out). The listing carries no per-entry trust annotation, because there is no longer a path by which an author-chosen URL can appear in it: a missing dependency comes from the index, and an upgrade reinstalls from the source that plugin's own install already accepted. A declined plan is a warning, not a failure. Dependencies already satisfied from raw `$PATH` or a local-dev install count as satisfied, with a warning when `min_version` can't be verified.
docs/architecture/external-commands.md:159:- `entire plugin doctor` reports missing/outdated dependencies, manifest/bin-dir drift, binaries that no longer match the `binary_sha256` recorded at install, installs that were never checksum-verified, dangling local-dev symlinks, and (macOS) a `com.apple.quarantine` attribute that would block execution. Description:
Problem:
Pi's extension was forwarding session lifecycle events (input, session_start, etc.) to Entire for all Pi processes, including nested subagents spawned by the tool system. This caused subagent sessions to be tracked separately as independent user sessions, breaking the model that only the top-level Pi should manage checkpoint lifecycle.
Solution:
Detect nested Pi processes by checking and setting the ENTIRE_PI_NESTED environment variable. Skip all session lifecycle forwarding (input events, session hooks) when running as a nested subagent, while still applying TTY hardening for bash calls in both parent and nested contexts. Only the top-level Pi now drives checkpoints and session state in Entire.

content.text:
`local_dev` is fully removed, `fmt`/`lint`/`test:ci` all pass.

## What changed

**The vulnerability is closed.** `local_dev` was honored from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json`, so any repo could commit `local_dev: true` and have `entire enable` install hooks that execute that repo's own `scripts/entire-dev`. Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. The struct field survives as a documented no-op — deleting it outright would hard-fail every existing config, since the loaders use `DisallowUnknownFields` (matching the `Strategy` precedent at `settings.go:153`). It's dropped from `mergeScalarFields`, so nothing reads it.

**Removed:** `--local-dev` flags (including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`, `scripts/entire-dev`, the `localDev` param from `InstallHooks` across all 9 agents plus the external-agent protocol, and the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout.

**Kept deliberately:** the legacy command prefixes in each agent's `entireHookPrefixes`. That's what lets `InstallHooks` recognize an old local-dev hook as *ours* and replace it. For opencode/pi I did the opposite and *removed* the legacy render from the freshness check — there, including it marked a legacy file as current, so it would never be rewritten.

## Three real bugs found while doing this

These are why the removal alone wouldn't have disarmed existing machines:

1. **cursor, factoryaidroid, claudecode, copilotcli only removed Entire hooks under `--force`.** A plain `entire enable` would *add* the binary hook while leaving the legacy dev-launcher hook in place — both fire, and the repo-relative one keeps running. Now stale Entire hooks are stripped unconditionally. The write also has to happen when nothing was *added* (a machine can hold both hooks at once), so the stripper reports whether it changed anything.
2. **geminicli's idempotency check sampled only `SessionStart`.** If that hook was current, it returned before the remove-and-add cycle, so a stale hook on any of the other 10 types survived every non-force install indefinitely.
3. **This repo's own committed agent configs all invoked the deleted script** — `.claude/settings.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, `.gemini/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, plus the pi/opencode files, all tracked. Left alone, this PR would have shipped a repo whose hooks point at a file that no longer exists. Regenerated through the real `InstallHooks`.

## On trail 1045 — still needed, and now done

Its premise was real: the committed pi extension was missing the entire `ENTIRE_PI_NESTED` subagent guard that's in the template. My change forced the issue, since its `ENTIRE_CMD` pointed at the deleted script. Both dogfood files are regenerated, and I added `AssertCommittedDogfoodFile` so CI catches this drift instead of a human noticing months later — verified it fails on drift and passes when correct. Worth closing the trail.

Note the trail's title and description don't match: the body describes nested-Pi detection (already implemented), not regeneration.

## Two things to know

- **`.claude/settings.json` is regenerated**, so this session's hooks now use `entire` from PATH rather than the dev launcher. Your next Claude Code session picks that up.
- **`absolute_git_hook_path` is the same shape of lever** — read from merged settings including the tracked project file, with `common.go` silently reinstalling git hooks from it. Far more benign (it inlines `os.Executable()`, not repo content), but the rule worth adopting is: no tracked setting may influence hook command generation. I left it as-is since scoping it is a separate behavior change.

I also retargeted `setup_test.go`'s scope-isolation coverage from `local_dev` to `absolute_git_hook_path` rather than deleting it — those tests prove a local-only override doesn't leak into the committed file, which is still worth testing. (`log_level` doesn't work there; it's already the project file's own field in those fixtures.)

Nothing is committed yet — the diff is 60 files, ready for you to review.

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

`absolute_git_hook_path` is still merged from the committed project file and still reaches `hookCmdPrefix`. But it only selects between `"entire"` and `shellQuote(os.Executable())` — the path of the binary already running. A repo cannot use it to make a hook execute repo content, so the security invariant ("hooks never run tracked content") is intact; what survives is a repo influencing the *form* of the command. It matches existing house precedent (`Strategy` at `:165`, `Review`/`ReviewFixAgent` at `:178-182` — all deprecated no-op fields kept for `DisallowUnknownFields` tolerance), so no new mechanism is warranted here. One inconsistency: the base-file struct decode (`loadFromFile`) **does** still populate `LocalDev` from the committed `.entire/settings.json`; only `mergeScalarFields` skips it. **Overall:** the core simplification is at the right altitude — collapsing `localDev bool` out of the `HookSupport` contract, deleting the launcher, and making `hookCmdPrefix`/`renderPlugin`/`renderExtension` unconditional is the deep version of this change, and the interface-level comment plus the guarded-prefix test are the right places to pin it. # Agent Integration Checklist

This document provides requirements and a checklist for integrating new AI coding agents with Entire. Use this to validate your implementation is correct and complete.

For step-by-step implementation instructions, code templates, and testing patterns, see the [Agent Implementation Guide](agent-guide.md).

## Core Principle: Full Transcript Storage

Entire stores the **complete session transcript** at every checkpoint, not incremental diffs. This enables:

- Simple rewind: restore the full transcript, agent resumes from that state
- No dependency on previous checkpoints being intact
- Consistent behavior across all checkpoint types (committed, uncommitted)

**Each checkpoint must contain the full session history up to that point.**

## Core Principle: Native Format Preservation

Store transcripts in the **agent's native format**. Any transformation or normalization should only be done to support CLI features (rewind, resume, summarization, file extraction), not for backend or web UI consumption.

**Why:**
- The backend/web UI should handle format differences, not the CLI
- Transforming for downstream consumers couples the CLI to their requirements
- Native formats ensure compatibility with agent's own import/export tools
- Reduces risk of data loss from lossy transformations
- Format changes that break the UI can be fixed with a backend deploy; CLI changes require a full release cycle and user adoption

**Do:**
- Store the raw transcript as the agent produces it
- Parse the native format when CLI features need specific data (e.g., extract file paths for `entire status`)
- Let the backend normalize formats for display

**Don't:**
- Create a "universal transcript format" in the CLI
- Transform logs to match what the web UI expects
- Strip or restructure data to simplify backend processing
- Create intermediate formats (e.g., converting JSON to JSONL for "easier parsing")
- Reconstruct transcripts from events when a canonical export exists

## Integration Checklist

### Transcript Capture

See Guide: [Transcript Format Guide](agent-guide.md#transcript-format-guide), [TranscriptAnalyzer](agent-guide.md#transcriptanalyzer), [TranscriptPreparer](agent-guide.md#transcriptpreparer)

- [ ] **Full transcript on every turn**: At turn-end, capture the complete session transcript, not just events since the last checkpoint
- [ ] **Resumed session handling**: When a user resumes an existing session, the transcript must include all historical messages, not just new ones since the plugin/hook loaded
- [ ] **Use agent's canonical export**: Prefer the agent's native export command (e.g., reading Claude's JSONL file, Gemini's JSON, Cursor's JSONL, Factory AI Droid's JSONL, Copilot CLI's JSONL, OpenCode's `opencode export` JSON, Pi's JSONL session file) over manually reconstructing from events
- [ ] **No custom formats**: Store the agent's native format directly in `NativeData` - do not convert between formats (e.g., JSON to JSONL) or create intermediate representations
- [ ] **Graceful degradation**: If the canonical source is unavailable (e.g., agent shutting down), fall back to best-effort capture with clear documentation of limitations

### Session Storage Abstraction

See Guide: [Step 3 - Core Agent Interface](agent-guide.md#step-3-implement-core-agent-interface-youragentgo)

- [ ] **`WriteSession` implementation**: Agent must implement `WriteSession(AgentSession)` to restore sessions
- [ ] **File-based agents** (Claude, Gemini, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi): Write `NativeData` to `SessionRef` path
- [ ] **Database-backed agents** (OpenCode): Write `NativeData` to file, then import into native storage (the native format should be what the agent's import command expects)
- [ ] **Single format per agent**: Store only the agent's native format in `NativeData` - no separate fields for different representations of the same data

### Hook Events

See Guide: [Step 4 - ParseHookEvent](agent-guide.md#step-4-implement-parsehookevent-lifecyclego), [Event Mapping Reference](agent-guide.md#event-mapping-reference)

Map agent-native hooks to these `EventType` constants (see `agent/event.go`):

- [ ] **TurnStart**: Fire when user submits a prompt (for pre-prompt state capture)
- [ ] **TurnEnd**: Fire when agent finishes responding (for checkpoint creation)
- [ ] **SessionStart**: Fire when a new session begins
- [ ] **SessionEnd**: Fire when session is explicitly ended (optional but recommended)

### Rewind/Resume Support

- [ ] **Rewind restores full state**: After rewind, agent can continue from that point with full context
- [ ] **Resume command**: `FormatResumeCommand()` returns the CLI command to resume a session
- [ ] **Session ID preservation**: Restored sessions maintain original session ID where possible

### Testing

See Guide: [Testing Patterns](agent-guide.md#testing-patterns)

- [ ] **New session**: Create session, multiple turns, verify full transcript at each checkpoint
- [ ] **Resumed session**: Resume existing session, add turns, verify checkpoint includes historical messages
- [ ] **Rewind**: Rewind to earlier checkpoint, verify agent can continue from that state
- [ ] **Agent shutdown**: Verify graceful handling if agent exits during checkpoint
- [ ] **Manual token validation for session-wide aggregate agents**: If an agent emits authoritative token totals only at session end (for example Copilot CLI `session.shutdown`), manually verify checkpoint-scoped metadata and full-session status separately. See [Copilot Token Validation](copilot-token-validation.md).

input.command:
cd /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-remove-local-dev
git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode

Local-dev mode pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher
inside the working tree that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was
read from the *committed* `.entire/settings.json` (settings.go merged
`local_dev` from the project scope, and strategy/common.go regenerated the git
hook from it), so any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have
`entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code. A branch
checkout could then swap what ran. This repo shipped exactly that: `local_dev:
true` was tracked, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary. Removed the `--local-dev` flags
(including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`,
the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and
the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and
the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented no-op: the loaders use
DisallowUnknownFields, so deleting the field would make every existing settings
file containing `local_dev` a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides
and nothing reads it, matching the `Strategy` precedent.

Removing the feature is not enough to disarm existing installs, so this also
fixes how hooks written by older versions get replaced:

- `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` only looked for the Entire marker, which a
  legacy hook still carries. It therefore read as installed forever and
  EnsureSetup never reinstalled it — while the script it invoked no longer
  existed. Repo-relative prefixes got no availability guard and pre-push
  deliberately propagates exit codes, so that state rejects `git push`. A hook
  naming the legacy launcher now counts as not installed.
- claudecode, factoryaidroid and copilotcli only dropped Entire hooks under
  `--force`, so a plain enable added the current hook beside the legacy one and
  both fired. cursor and codex returned early whenever the current command was
  present, leaving a legacy hook next to it. Stale hooks are now dropped on
  every install, through one shared `agent.DropStaleManagedHooks` primitive
  rather than six per-agent re-derivations (`dupl` cannot see duplication across
  packages, which is how the two divergent copies survived).
- geminicli's idempotency check sampled only SessionStart, so a stale hook on
  any of the other ten types survived every non-force install.
- The write now happens when only a drop occurred: a config can hold both a
  stale and a current hook, where nothing needs adding.
- Every hook prefix is guarded by an existence test. The unguarded path existed
  only for the repo-relative launcher, and was still reachable for unusual
  absolute paths — exactly where losing the guard hurts most.

Regenerates this repo's six committed agent configs through the real install
path. The pi extension had also drifted far enough to be missing the
ENTIRE_PI_NESTED subagent guard that was already in its template, so
`testutil.AssertCommittedDogfoodFile` and `AssertCommittedDogfoodConfigStable`
now fail in CI on drift instead of waiting for someone to notice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

cd /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-remove-local-dev
gh pr create --title "refactor(hooks)!: remove local_dev mode" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Why

`local_dev` pointed installed hooks at `scripts/entire-dev`, a launcher **inside the working tree** that compiled and ran the checked-out source. It was read from the **committed** `.entire/settings.json` — `mergeScalarFields` merged `local_dev` from project scope, and `strategy/common.go` regenerated the git hook from it — so **any repository could commit `"local_dev": true` and have `entire enable` install hooks that execute that repository's own code.** A branch checkout then swapped what ran.

This was live here, not hypothetical: `local_dev: true` was tracked in this repo, and all six committed agent configs invoked the launcher.

Hooks now always name the `entire` binary.

## Removed

`--local-dev` flags (including the non-hidden one on `entire agent add`), `EnableOptions.LocalDev`, the `localDev` parameter from `Agent.InstallHooks` across all nine agents and the external-agent protocol, the claude-code local-dev SessionEnd timeout, and the launcher script.

`EntireSettings.LocalDev` stays as a documented **no-op**. The loaders use `DisallowUnknownFields`, so deleting the field would turn every existing settings file containing `local_dev` into a hard parse error. It is not merged from overrides and nothing reads it — same shape as the existing `Strategy` field.

## Removing the feature was not enough to disarm existing installs

Five separate defects meant hooks written by older versions would have survived. Each is fixed:

| Defect | Consequence |
| --- | --- |
| `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` only checked the Entire marker, which legacy hooks still carry | Read as installed forever, so `EnsureSetup` never reinstalled — while invoking a script that no longer exists. Repo-relative prefixes get no availability guard and `pre-push` propagates exit codes, so this state **rejects `git push`** |
| claudecode / factoryaidroid / copilotcli only dropped Entire hooks under `--force` | Plain enable added the current hook *beside* the legacy one — both fire |
| cursor / codex returned early whenever the current command was present | Legacy hook left sitting next to it |
| geminicli's idempotency check sampled only `SessionStart` | A stale hook on any of the other ten types survived every non-force install |
| The write was skipped when only a drop occurred | A config holding both a stale and a current hook needs no *addition*, so the drop was discarded |

Stale-hook handling now routes through one shared `agent.DropStaleManagedHooks` primitive instead of six per-agent re-derivations. `dupl` cannot see duplication across packages, which is how the two divergent copies survived unnoticed.

Every hook prefix is now guarded by an existence test. The unguarded path existed only for the repo-relative launcher and was still reachable for unusual absolute paths — exactly where losing the guard hurts most.

## Verified against reality

While committing this, the repo's own clone turned out to carry an **older** legacy shape (`go run ./cmd/entire/main.go`) rather than `scripts/entire-dev`, which the first version of the migration check missed. Detection now covers both forms that ever ran Entire from the working tree.

## Dogfood configs

Regenerates this repo's six committed agent configs through the real install path. The pi extension had drifted far enough to be **missing the `ENTIRE_PI_NESTED` subagent guard already present in its template** — closing [trail #1045](https://entire.io/gh/entireio/cli/trails/1045). `testutil.AssertCommittedDogfoodFile` and `AssertCommittedDogfoodConfigStable` now fail in CI on drift rather than waiting for someone to notice.

## Performance note

Production hook command strings are unchanged. For anyone previously on local-dev — everyone working in this repo — per-hook-firing cost drops from **~4s to ~4ms**: the old path ran `git rev-parse`, then `go build`, then `go run` on every agent turn and every git operation.

## Follow-ups deliberately not in scope

- `absolute_git_hook_path` is still merged from the committed project file and still influences hook *form*. It cannot make a hook run repo content (it only selects between bare `entire` and `os.Executable()`), so the security invariant holds — but the general rule worth adopting is that no tracked setting influences hook command generation.
- A format-agnostic cross-agent contract test over every `HookSupport` agent (the shared primitive makes this cheap now, and it would have caught cursor/codex).
- An `env.RunGit` harness helper: `core.hooksPath` isolation is applied at one call site, and ~70 raw `git` invocations in the integration package are latently exposed now that hooks resolve `entire` through PATH.

## Testing

`mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci` all pass. Each new guard was verified to actually fail on the defect it protects against (reverted the fix, watched it fail, restored).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

content.text:
Committed and shipped: **https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1999** (63 files, +1745/−1280).

## What the /simplify pass changed

Four agents ran in parallel. The efficiency pass found nothing to fix and instead quantified the win (production hook strings unchanged; ~4s → ~3.8ms per hook firing for anyone previously on local-dev). The other three found ~30 issues that deduped into one regression, two real bugs, one consolidation, and cleanups.

**One regression my earlier work introduced.** `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` only checked the Entire marker, which legacy hooks still carry — so they read as installed forever, `EnsureSetup` never migrated them, and they invoked the script I'd deleted. Unguarded prefix + `pre-push` propagating exit codes = **`git push` rejected**. Fixed and tested.

**Two real bugs.** cursor and codex returned early whenever the current command was present, leaving a legacy hook beside it — the exact state I'd added a test for in claudecode. My earlier claim that those two were "already correct" held only for the legacy-only case. Fixed, and I verified each test fails on the original code and passes on the fix.

**The consolidation.** Six per-agent re-derivations of "drop our stale hooks" became one `agent.DropStaleManagedHooks` primitive. `dupl` can't see across packages, which is how the two wrong copies survived. This also fixed the two bugs structurally rather than per-agent, and removed the `staleHookDropSpec` pointer-to-slice indirection I'd added — an agent empirically confirmed the simpler closure form lints clean, so that struct bought nothing.

**Also fixed:** geminicli's idempotency check sampled only `SessionStart`, so stale hooks on the other ten types survived every non-force install. `GeneratedHookFileState`'s doc I'd rewritten said "including any left by older versions" — the exact opposite of what the tests pin. Five duplicated ~50-line migration tests collapsed into `agent/testutil` helpers. The `!ok` unguarded-hook path is gone. Dogfood drift guards extended from 2 of 6 configs to all 6. A dead `writeProductionHookSettings` was silently dropping `filtered_fetches`.

## One thing worth knowing

While committing, this clone turned out to carry an *older* legacy shape — `go run ./cmd/entire/main.go`, not `scripts/entire-dev` — which my first migration check missed entirely. Detection now covers both forms, verified against this clone's actual hook content. That's a good argument for the follow-ups below: the fix was correct in shape but I'd guessed at the population.

## Skipped, with reasons

- **`absolute_git_hook_path`** is still merged from the committed project file and influences hook form. It can't make a hook run repo content, so the invariant holds — but scoping it is a separate behavior change.
- **Cross-agent contract test** over every `HookSupport` agent — cheap now that the primitive is shared, and it would have caught cursor/codex.
- **`env.RunGit` harness helper** — I isolated `core.hooksPath` at one call site; ~70 raw `git` invocations in the integration package are latently exposed now that hooks resolve `entire` through PATH. Worth doing before more are added.
- **Converting claudecode's two migration tests** to the shared helper — cosmetic; its bespoke versions pass and are more specific.

All three are in the PR body as follow-ups. `mise run fmt && mise run lint && mise run test:ci` pass; CI on the PR hasn't reported yet.

content.text:
Both commits are on **PR #1999**. Your instinct was right — and the answer turned out stronger than a type tweak.

## What the comment was hiding

Once I looked, `LegacyLocalDevHookScript`'s only *production* uses were those five detection lists. Every other reference was a comment or a test. So it never needed to be exported at all — the comment was load-bearing purely because the constant was reachable.

## The change

The recognized set moved **unexported** into the agent package, and both `IsManagedHookCommand` and `DropStaleManagedHooks` lost their `prefixes` parameter:

```go
const currentHookCommandPrefix = "entire "

// DETECTION-ONLY, and unexported so that is enforced rather than documented.
var legacyHookCommandPrefixes = []string{...}
```

Verified the enforcement holds by trying both escape routes from `cursor`:

```
undefined: agent.LegacyLocalDevHookScript
undefined: agent.legacyHookCommandPrefixes
```

Compile errors, not convention violations. Tests that need to *build* a legacy command (to seed a config an older version wrote) go through `agent/testutil`, which is test-only by construction — so the capability exists exactly where it's legitimate.

## Two things that fell out of it

Dropping the parameter was only possible because **every agent's current prefix was already the same bare `"entire "`** — the parameter had no remaining purpose. That let the six per-agent `entireHookPrefixes` literals go away: five were byte-identical, and claudecode differed only in resolving the repo root via `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}` instead of git. The shared set now covers all four shapes Entire has ever written, matched for every agent.

That closes a follow-up I'd deferred: a newly added agent now **inherits** legacy detection rather than having to remember to copy the list. Omitting those entries is precisely what leaves an old hook installed forever, and it's the kind of omission `dupl` can't catch (it doesn't cross package boundaries — which is how the two divergent copies survived in the first place).

Net: −144/+107 lines, `fmt`/`lint`/`test:ci` all pass.

One asymmetry worth noting: the git-hook side has its own `legacyGitHookLaunchers` in `strategy/hooks.go`, already unexported but a separate list. Unifying the two would mean the strategy package importing agent (or a shared home for "shapes Entire has written"). I left it alone — it's a real duplication of *knowledge*, but small, and both copies are now correctly scoped. Say the word if you'd rather it be one list.

content.text:
Cleaned up (tree clean, no leftover worktree). Here's the verified answer — and it splits by which legacy era your clone's hooks are from.

## Your case: `go run` hooks — nothing breaks

1. **The pull doesn't touch them.** `.git/hooks/*` are per-clone and untracked, so they stay `go run ./cmd/entire/main.go hooks git …`.
2. **They keep working.** I need to correct something I said earlier: `go run ./cmd/entire/main.go` *does* still build — `cmd/entire/` contains only `main.go`. So those hooks run the freshly pulled source. Slow (~4s per firing) and still executing repo content, but functional. All five carry `|| true`, so even a missing Go toolchain just no-ops.
3. **The committed agent hooks DO update** via the pull — `.claude/settings.json` etc. become `sh -c 'if ! command -v entire …; exec entire …'`, so they invoke the newly installed binary from PATH.
4. **First turn-start migrates the git hooks.** `handleLifecycleTurnStart` → `EnsureSetup` → `IsGitHookInstalled` sees `go run ` → returns false → `InstallGitHook` rewrites all five. Verified end-to-end in a scratch repo:

```
before: go run ./cmd/entire/main.go hooks git pre-push "$1" || true
after:  if command -v entire >/dev/null 2>&1; then entire hooks git pre-push "$1"; else :; fi
```

Note this fires on the first turn of a **new** session after the pull — Claude Code reads `.claude/settings.json` at session start.

## The other era: `scripts/entire-dev` hooks — `git push` breaks first

This one I'd rather you know about than discover. I built the pre-merge binary from `main` and generated hooks with `local_dev: true`. That era emitted:

```
./scripts/entire-dev hooks git pre-push "$1"
```

**Unguarded, and no `|| true`** — because `gitHookCommandAvailableTest` returned `ok=false` for a repo-relative prefix, and pre-push deliberately propagates exit codes for OPF. Your pull *deletes* that tracked script, so:

```
.git/hooks/pre-push: line 5: ./scripts/entire-dev: No such file or directory
error: failed to push some refs
```

Reproduced, then confirmed the recovery: one turn-start with the new binary rewrote the hook and the push succeeded. So `entire enable` or any agent turn heals it — but a `pull` → `push` with no session in between fails.

## What I'd suggest

The window is real and narrows to zero after any agent turn, but it lands on exactly the people who had `local_dev` on — this repo's team. Two options:

1. **Release note** — "if you used local-dev hooks, start a session or run `entire enable` after upgrading." Zero code.
2. **Give `entire doctor` a git-hook check.** It currently has *none* (only agent `CheckHookConfig` + codex trust), and doctor is literally the scan-and-fix flow. The predicate already exists, so it's a small addition and puts the repair where a user in trouble would look.

I'd do both — (2) is ~20 lines and closes the gap properly rather than relying on a note being read. Want me to add it to the PR?

content.text:
Added to **PR #1999** (3 commits, 64 files). CI is running.

## The test

`cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/local_dev_migration_test.go` — integration-level, driving the real binary through the harness's `SimulateUserPromptSubmit`, so it exercises the actual `turn-start → EnsureSetup → IsGitHookInstalled → InstallGitHook` chain rather than the predicate in isolation.

**`TestLocalDevMigration_TurnStartReplacesLegacyGitHooks`** — table-driven over both legacy eras. Seeds all five managed hooks in a legacy shape *with* Entire's marker (the detail that made them survive), asserts they don't read as installed, fires one turn-start, then checks every hook invokes the binary, is PATH-guarded, and contains no `scripts/entire-dev`, `go run `, or `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`.

**`TestLocalDevMigration_LauncherEraPushIsRepaired`** — the user-visible symptom. It **reproduces the push rejection before asserting the repair**, so it can't pass without having actually hit the bug.

Two traps I had to avoid there, both of which would have made it vacuous:

- `SetupBareRemote` already pushes HEAD, and **git skips pre-push entirely when a push is a no-op** — so the hook would never have run. It now commits through `go-git` (which fires no hooks, so it can't trip the broken one) to give the push something to send.
- The harness's `GitPushWithHooks` fatals on error *and* reinstalls its own pre-push hook. Both defeat the point, so there's a small local push helper that returns the outcome and leaves the seeded hook alone.

## Verified it catches the bug

A passing test proves nothing on its own, so I removed the legacy-launcher detection from `isGitHookInstalledInHooksDir` and confirmed both fail:

```
--- FAIL: TestLocalDevMigration_TurnStartReplacesLegacyGitHooks
    legacy local-dev hooks must not count as installed, or EnsureSetup never migrates them   (×2 eras)
--- FAIL: TestLocalDevMigration_LauncherEraPushIsRepaired
    hook pre-push still reaches into the working tree ("scripts/entire-dev")   (×5 hooks)
```

Then restored `hooks.go` byte-identical and re-confirmed green. `fmt`/`lint`/`test:ci` all pass.

One small guard worth mentioning: `seedLegacyGitHooks` fails loudly if a managed hook has no recorded legacy argument list, so adding a sixth git hook can't silently drop it from this coverage.

**Still open from before:** the `entire doctor` git-hook check. This test pins that migration works, but a user who pulls and pushes *before* starting a session still hits the rejection once — doctor is where they'd look, and it currently has no git-hook check at all. Say the word and I'll add it.

cd /Users/soph/.herdr/worktrees/cli/soph-remove-local-dev
git add -A
git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(doctor): check and repair stale git hooks

`.git/hooks` is the one hook surface a user cannot see going wrong. Agent hook
configs are committed files that turn up in a diff; git hooks are per-clone and
untracked, so pulling a release that changes hook generation never touches them.
A hook left by the removed local-dev mode still carries Entire's marker, so it
looks installed while naming a launcher inside the working tree that is gone —
and because that shape got no availability guard while pre-push propagates exit
codes, the symptom is `git push` being rejected. Doctor had no git-hook check at
all, so the place a user looks after a rejected push said nothing.

Unlike the sibling agent hook checks this one repairs rather than only warning:
the reinstall is content-idempotent, backs up any foreign hook it displaces, and
writes exactly what the next turn-start would write anyway. It degrades to
warn-only when there is nobody to ask, naming `--force` instead — doctor is a
diagnostic an agent or CI job runs unattended, so it must neither block on a
confirm nor rewrite a repo's hooks unasked. An existing bare-`doctor` test caught
that: without the guard the prompt fails to open a TTY and doctor exits 1.

Distinguishing "no hooks" from "ours but stale" needs more than a bool, so this
adds strategy.GitHookState (Absent/Current/Outdated), mirroring
agent.HookConfigState so both hook surfaces share one vocabulary.
IsGitHookInstalled keeps meaning "current" for EnsureSetup.

That tri-state also fixes a regression from the local_dev removal: runUninstall
used IsGitHookInstalled both for its "nothing to uninstall" early return and to
decide whether to remove hooks. Once a legacy hook stopped counting as installed,
a repo whose only Entire artifact was such a hook reported "Entire is not
installed" and left it behind. Uninstall now asks AnyGitHookInstalled — a stale
hook is still ours, and still ours to remove.

ReinstallGitHooks exports the settings-lookup-plus-install pair EnsureSetup
already ran, so callers outside the package cannot open-code it and silently drop
absolute_git_hook_path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
